objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain every class and type of airspace with its weather, radio, equipment and pilot rules, special VFR, special use airspace, TFRs, SFRAs and chart currency, and teach it so a student can read the sectional, plan a legal route and stay inside the student pilot limits.
why: Airspace is where a student first meets rules the airplane cannot warn about: a line on a chart, a TFR, an expired chart. The AIH lists TFRs and special use airspace among the items an instructor must cover [[25:164|AIH 8-6]], and your endorsement is what lets a student fly solo in Class B or to an airport inside it [[60:287|14 CFR 61.95]]. Teach it so it sticks, because the student will fly it alone.

warmup: Think first: your student has 12 hours and can recite the VFR minimums table without a mistake. On the sectional you point to a blue dashed circle with a boxed -30, sitting under a solid magenta ring, and ask: what is this, what do you need to fly into it, and what is above it? The student freezes. What level of learning has the student reached, and what will you change in the next airspace lesson?

chunks.title: K1: Build the big picture first: categories, types and classes

body.p: Start with the frame, not the details. Airspace has two categories, regulatory and nonregulatory, and four types: controlled, uncontrolled, special use and other airspace [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]]. What sets them is the density of traffic, the kind of operations, the level of safety needed and the national and public interest [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]]. Give the student that reason first: busy places get more rules.

bullets: Controlled: Class A, B, C, D and E. ATC gives service to IFR and VFR flights according to the class [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].
Uncontrolled: Class G, which is everything not designated A, B, C, D or E [[33:189|AIM 3-3-1]]. ATC has no authority to control traffic there, but VFR minimums still apply [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].
Regulatory: Class A to E plus restricted and prohibited areas. Nonregulatory: MOAs, warning, alert, controlled firing and national security areas [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].
Overlap: when two designations cover the same airspace, the rules of the more restrictive one apply. A is most restrictive, then B, C, D, E, and G is least [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]].

callout.text: Teach it: the AIH uses airspace as its own example of simple-to-complex. If a learner flies only in Class D, E and G, save A, B and C until the learner is familiar with the ones in use [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Application: the exception is any airspace the learner meets on the first solo, because the pre-solo knowledge test must cover the airspace rules and procedures for the solo airport [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(b)]].

The AIH says similar material interferes with memory more than different material, and material not learned well suffers most [[25:89|AIH 3-38]]. Classes B, C and D look alike to a new student. Teach them side by side in one table so the differences, not the look-alikes, are what the student stores.

check.q: Your student asks why a restricted area is 'regulatory' but a MOA is not. What do you say?
check.a: Prohibited and restricted areas are regulatory SUA set up by rulemaking in 14 CFR part 73; MOAs, warning, alert, controlled firing and national security areas are nonregulatory [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1]]. So a VFR pilot may enter an active MOA with extreme caution [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]], but may not enter a restricted area contrary to its restrictions without permission [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].

body.p: Class B pilot rules are where your signature matters. A student pilot may fly solo in Class B only after ground and flight training on that specific Class B area, with the flight training given in that area, and with a logbook endorsement from the instructor who gave the flight training, dated within the 90 days before the flight [[60:287|14 CFR 61.95(a)]]. Solo flight to, from or at an airport inside Class B needs the same, given at that specific airport [[60:287|14 CFR 61.95(b)]]. AC 61-65K gives sample wording for both endorsements [[12:42|AC 61-65K A-9]].

callout.text: No endorsement opens the airports in Part 91 Appendix D, section 4: solo student, sport and recreational pilot operations are not permitted there. The list includes Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson, Boston Logan, Chicago O'Hare, Dallas/Fort Worth, Los Angeles, Miami, Newark, JFK, LaGuardia, San Francisco, Reagan National and Joint Base Andrews [[60:650|14 CFR Part 91 App. D]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)(2)]].

Figure 15-9 is a summary, not the rule. It puts ADS-B Out in a footnote and boils the student rule down to one line. When a student quotes the figure, send them to the regulations themselves [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]] [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]].

Teach it: before the first dual flight into Class B, have the student write down what a clearance into the Class Bravo sounds like. In flight, use learner tells, instructor does: the student tells you what to say and you make the call. A misunderstanding gets fixed before the student is also busy flying the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: A student holds your 61.95(a) endorsement for the Atlanta Class B and asks to make a solo landing at Hartsfield-Jackson. Can you endorse it?
check.a: No. Hartsfield-Jackson is in Part 91 Appendix D, section 4, where solo student pilot operations are not permitted, whatever the training [[60:650|14 CFR Part 91 App. D]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)(2)]].

chunks.title: K1: Class D, E and G, and towered airports without Class D

bullets: Class D: generally from the surface to 2,500 feet above the airport, around an airport with an operating control tower [[33:185|AIM 3-2-5]]. Two-way radio communication before entry, no specific certificate [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]], and no separation for VFR aircraft [[33:187|AIM 3-2-5]].

Part-time Class D: the hours are in the Chart Supplement, and when the tower closes the surface area becomes Class E or Class G; the Chart Supplement says 'other times CLASS E' or 'other times CLASS G' [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

Class E: controlled airspace for terminal or en route purposes, with no specific certificate and no entry requirement [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]]. A Class E surface area needs weather reporting and radio coverage down to the runway [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]]. Transition areas begin at 700 or 1,200 feet AGL and stay in effect at all times, whatever the airport hours [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]]. Federal airways run from 1,200 feet AGL up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].
Class E where no lower base is charted: from 14,500 feet MSL up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL, but not within 1,500 feet of the surface unless designated lower [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].
Class G: uncontrolled airspace, everything not designated A to E [[33:189|AIM 3-3-1]], but the 91.155 minimums still apply [[33:189|AIM 3-3-2]].

callout.text: A working tower is a radio rule in any class. To, from, through or on an airport with an operating control tower, keep two-way radio with the tower, established before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]] [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127(c)]]. If the radio fails under VFR in Class D, you may land with basic VFR weather, visual contact with the tower and a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]].

For C and D, listen for your own call sign. The controller using it, even with 'standby,' means contact is made and you may enter. A reply without your call sign, or 'remain outside,' means stay out [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

Teach it known to unknown [[25:113|AIH 5-10]]. Start with the home airport the student already knows: what class it is now, what it becomes after the tower closes, and where the magenta or blue vignette puts the Class E floor overhead [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

check.q: Your Class D home field's tower closes at 2200, and the Chart Supplement says 'other times CLASS G.' The field sits inside a magenta vignette. At 2230, what is the airspace from the surface up?
check.a: Class G from the surface up to, but not including, the overlying controlled airspace, which is normally the Class E transition area beginning at 700 feet AGL where a magenta vignette is charted [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

chunks.title: K1 and S2: Transponder and ADS-B Out, the rules students mix up

body.p: Students learn 'Mode C in B and C' and stop there. The rules reach further. Teach them as one list of places where an altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out are both required [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]]:

bullets: Class A, B and C airspace. In Class A the ADS-B Out must meet TSO-C166b or C166c [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(1)]] [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]], which the AIM calls 1090ES equipment [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]].
Within 30 NM of a Part 91 Appendix D, section 1 airport, from the surface up to 10,000 feet MSL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(2)]].
Above the ceiling and inside the lateral limits of a Class B or Class C area, up to 10,000 feet MSL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(4)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(3)]].
At and above 10,000 feet MSL over the 48 states and DC, except at and below 2,500 feet AGL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]].
ADS-B Out only: Class E at and above 3,000 feet MSL over the Gulf within 12 NM of the coast [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(5)]] [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].

body.p: In all controlled airspace, a working installed transponder must be on, with Mode C, replying on the right code [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]]. ADS-B Out transmits at all times unless ATC directs otherwise [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(f)]]. Under VFR the code is 1200 unless ATC assigns another [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]].

A student who plans only from the chart will miss them. Make the student say them out loud during every planning session.

check.q: On a dual flight 20 NM from a Class B primary airport, inside the 30 NM veil, your trainer's transponder fails. What can you legally do?
check.a: Ask ATC for a deviation. For an inoperative transponder going to the destination or to a repair shop, the request may be made at any time [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(2)]]. Without an authorization you may not keep operating in the veil [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]].

bullets: Night exception, Class G below 1,200 feet AGL: with at least 1 SM but less than 3 SM, an airplane may fly clear of clouds in the traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]].

Surface areas: no VFR beneath a ceiling of less than 1,000 feet, except special VFR [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]. To take off, land or enter the pattern you need 3 SM ground visibility, or 3 SM flight visibility if none is reported [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]].
At the exact base of a Class E area, you count as being in the airspace below it [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]].

callout.text: Student pilots have a floor of their own on top of the table: no acting as PIC with flight or surface visibility under 3 SM by day or 5 SM at night, or when the flight cannot be made with visual reference to the surface [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(6),(7)]]. The AIM points to this rule right under its minimums [[33:176|AIM 3-1-4]]. So the 1 SM Class G day row never applies to your solo student.

A memory aid (application, not FAA wording): '3-152' for Class C, Class D and Class E below 10,000 feet MSL: 3 SM, 1,000 above, 500 below, 2,000 horizontal. In Class E at or above 10,000 MSL, and in Class G above 1,200 feet AGL at or above 10,000 MSL, it becomes '5-111': 5 SM, 1,000 above, 1,000 below, 1 SM horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. The AIH encourages mnemonics that tie new facts to things already known [[25:90|AIH 3-39]].

Teach it past rote. Repeating the table without being able to apply it is the lowest level of learning [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. Give a position, an altitude, a time of day and a METAR, and have the student pick the row and make the go or no-go call.

check.q: Day, Class G, 1,000 feet AGL, flight visibility 2 SM, clear of clouds. A private pilot and your solo student are both flying there. Who is legal?
check.a: The private pilot is legal: 1 SM and clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. The student is not: a student pilot may not act as PIC with less than 3 SM by day [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(6)]].

chunks.title: K5: Special VFR, and why it is not a student tool

body.p: Special VFR replaces the 91.155 minimums with lower ones, but only below 10,000 feet MSL, inside the upward extension of a surface area of controlled airspace, and not at the airports in Part 91 Appendix D, section 3 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(a)]].

Clear of clouds [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(2)]]

bullets: SVFR is given traffic permitting, when it will not delay IFR operations [[33:277|AIM 4-4-6]].
The clearance has no set altitude because you must stay clear of clouds, and you keep the job of obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].
Airports where fixed-wing SVFR is banned show 'NO SVFR' above the airport name on the chart [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].

callout.text: Application: a solo student pilot can never use the 1 SM SVFR visibility, because 61.89 still requires 3 SM by day and 5 SM at night [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(6)]]. Teach SVFR as a rule the student will use later, together with the judgment it needs: a clear-of-clouds, 1 SM clearance in a low-time pilot's hands invites flying lower and lower to stay out of cloud.

Teach it with two questions: 'What is the lowest legal weather?' and then 'What is your lowest weather?' Linking the rule to the student's own limits moves it from rote toward correlation, the level the AIH says should be the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

check.q: At night, a private pilot client asks you what it takes to get special VFR out of a Class D in an airplane. What does the rule require beyond the daytime SVFR rules?
check.a: Two things: the person granted the clearance must meet the applicable part 61 requirements for instrument flight, and the airplane must be equipped as 91.205(d) requires [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]]. Application: 91.157 does not list those part 61 sections; check the client against them, for example the instrument experience rule for acting as PIC in weather below VFR minimums [[60:239|14 CFR 61.57(c)]].

chunks.title: K2: Chart symbols, and teaching from the sectional

bullets: Class B: solid blue lines. Ceiling over floor in hundreds of feet MSL. A '+' before a floor means the floor is above that number, and operations at and below it are outside Class B [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

Class C: solid magenta lines and figures. A ceiling of 'T' means up to, but not including, the Class B floor above. Magenta boxes give the approach frequency to call, generally within 20 NM [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].
Class D: blue dashed line, ceiling in a box. A minus in front means from the surface up to, but not including, that value [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

Class E: surface area is a magenta dashed line. Magenta vignette means a 700-foot AGL floor; blue vignette means another floor next to Class G; other floors carry a number [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].
Mode C veil: a solid magenta 30 NM circle. Part 93 airports have their names boxed [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].
Airports with a control tower are blue; all others are magenta [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]].

body.p: The PHAK's sectional excerpt makes a good first teaching chart: one picture holds a Class C, towered and nontowered airports, restricted, warning and MOA areas, a Part 93 special air traffic rule box, the ADIZ, the chart legend and the edition dates on the cover [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]]. The PHAK reminds pilots that the legend explains most symbols and that the chart also lists ATC frequencies and airspace information [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]].

callout.text: Teach symbols on the ground first. The AIH describes a learner who tries to read unfamiliar chart symbols in flight and drifts off heading; the fix is more time on the chart skill by itself, because flying the airplane does nothing to teach chart symbols [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Then reinforce in the air: point out the real landmark the student marked as a boundary.
Near Class B, switch to the Terminal Area Chart. It has more detail, and the sectional marks where TAC coverage begins [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]] [[34:191|AIM 9-1-5]].

check.q: A Class D ceiling box reads '-32'. Where does the Class D stop, and what does the minus tell the student?
check.a: From the surface up to, but not including, 3,200 feet MSL; the minus means 'surface to, but not including' the value [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]]. Whatever airspace is drawn above it, often a Class C or B shelf, starts there.

bullets: On VFR charts, prohibited, restricted and warning areas are drawn in blue and MOAs and alert areas in magenta, and only the part below 18,000 feet MSL is shown [[2:45|Chart Users' Guide p.45]].

The chart's SUA tabulation lists altitudes, time of use and the controlling agency. No NOTAM is issued to announce the permanently listed times [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]]. SUA that needs a NOTAM to activate shows up in the ARTCC NOTAMs [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]].
Temporary MOAs, temporary restricted areas and controlled firing areas are not charted [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1]].

callout.text: The RMH names entering prohibited or restricted airspace without permission as an environment hazard that can cause conflicts with military aircraft [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Drill it until 'no NOTAM' never means 'not active' to your student.

check.q: Your student says: 'The MOA is hot, so it's illegal for us to go through.' Correct?
check.a: No. VFR pilots may fly through an active MOA, with extreme caution; get status from an FSS within 100 miles and traffic advisories from the controlling agency first [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]]. Whether you should is a risk decision, not a legal one.

chunks.title: K3 and S3: TFRs, SFRAs, special air traffic rules and other areas

body.p: A TFR is a type of NOTAM that restricts flight because of a hazard, a special event or a general warning, and only TFRs related to national security are charted [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]]. Knowing about TFRs on the route is the pilot's job; the PHAK suggests checking the FAA TFR website [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]], and the AIM says to check NOTAMs during flight planning [[33:195|AIM 3-5-3]].

head: TFR rule
Reason
Who may enter, or normal size
rows: Hazard from an incident on the surface
Only relief aircraft under the on-scene official [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(b)]]; normally within 2,000 feet above the surface and 3 NM [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3]]
Disaster relief aircraft
Relief aircraft, law enforcement, IFR flight plans, some airport traffic not there to observe, accredited news [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)]]
Sightseeing congestion
Airport traffic not there to observe, IFR flight plans, event staff, law enforcement, news with a flight plan [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(d)]] [[60:458|14 CFR 91.137(d)(4)]]
President, Vice President, other public figures
Only as the NOTAM allows [[60:459|14 CFR 91.141]]
Space flight operations
Only when ATC authorizes [[60:459|14 CFR 91.143]]
Aerial demonstration
Normally 5 NM and up to 17,000 feet MSL for high-performance aircraft (13,000 feet above the surface for some parachute operations) [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(1)]]
Major sporting event
Normally 3 NM and 2,500 feet above the surface [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(2)]]

body.p: Special air traffic rules (SATR) are the rules in 14 CFR part 93; some of those areas are also designated special flight rules areas (SFRA). Anyone flying to, from or within them follows part 93 unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[33:202|AIM 3-5-7]]. The one every student must know is the Washington DC SFRA: surface to, but not including, FL 180 within 30 miles of the DCA VOR/DME, with the Flight Restricted Zone (FRZ) inside it [[60:705|14 CFR 93.335]].

bullets: DC SFRA: working two-way radio and contact before entry, an altitude-reporting transponder squawking an ATC-assigned discrete code, and for VFR a DC SFRA or FRZ flight plan [[60:705|14 CFR 93.339(a)]]. Code 1200 is never allowed in the SFRA [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].
Special Awareness Training is required to fly VFR within 60 NM of the DCA VOR/DME, and the certificate must be shown on request [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161]].
Violations, even inadvertent ones, can bring civil penalties and certificate suspension or revocation [[60:704|14 CFR 93.333(a)]].

Military training routes: four digits means no segment above 1,500 feet AGL; three digits means at least one segment above [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2]]. A route can be several miles wide; in flight, ask an FSS within 100 NM about activity [[33:195|AIM 3-5-2]].

Published VFR routes: a flyway needs no clearance; a corridor is a hole through Class B with no clearance; a transition route needs ATC communication and, in Class B, a clearance [[33:198|AIM 3-5-5]] [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5]].
TRSA: not a class of airspace; VFR participation is voluntary [[33:201|AIM 3-5-6]]. Parachute jump areas are listed in the Chart Supplement [[33:197|AIM 3-5-4]].
Never charted: altitude reservations come by NOTAM and VFR may fly through with vigilance; no NOTAM announces activation of ATC assigned airspace [[33:203|AIM 3-5-10]].

callout.text: Teach it: TFRs and special use airspace are both on the AIH list of items instructors must cover [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. Make the TFR and NOTAM check part of every preflight, dual or solo, and have the student brief it to you before you look. The AIH says learners should help resolve training environment issues such as airspace, NOTAMs and TFRs [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: A student plans a VFR flight to an airport 50 NM from the DCA VOR/DME, outside the SFRA. What extra requirement applies?
check.a: Special Awareness Training and its completion certificate, because the flight is under VFR within 60 NM of the DCA VOR/DME [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161(a)]].

body.p: Aeronautical information changes fast. The Chart Users' Guide tells pilots to check the effective dates on every chart and publication, use current editions, and discard obsolete ones [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]]. The AIM urges using only the latest issue of charts [[33:322|AIM 5-1-1]]. Behind both stands the regulation: before every flight, the PIC must become familiar with all available information about that flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

head: Publication
How often it changes
rows: Sectional chart
Every 56 days [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]] [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]]
VFR Terminal Area Chart
Every 56 days [[34:191|AIM 9-1-5]]
Chart Supplement
Issued every 56 days [[34:199|AIM 9-1-5]]
Changes between editions
NOTAMs carry the updates essential for safe flight [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]]

bullets: To confirm a chart is current, read the next scheduled edition date printed on the cover. New information takes effect at 0901Z [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]].
Errors found after publication are announced as Safety Alerts; planned changes as Charting Notices [[34:190|AIM 9-1-3]].

GPS and tablet databases: check the currency. If one has expired and cannot be updated, disregard its moving-map airspace for critical navigation decisions and check waypoints against a current sectional or Chart Supplement [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].

callout.text: The PHAK still says sectionals and TACs are revised semiannually [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]]. The AIM and the Chart Users' Guide say every 56 days [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]] [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]]. Teach 56 days.

Teach it: have the student find the edition dates on the chart cover in the PHAK sectional figure [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]], then on their own chart or app, at every preflight. Model it yourself: the AIH says keeping a current library is the instructor's responsibility [[25:164|AIH 8-6]].

check.q: Your student's paper sectional shows a next edition date of yesterday. Is it still good for today's flight?
check.a: No. The new edition took effect at 0901Z on that date, so the old chart is obsolete; use the current edition and discard the old one [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]].

chunks.title: R1: Managing airspace risk, for the student and for you

body.p: The RMH treats airspace as part of the environment hazard: prohibited and restricted airspace, ATC delays and service availability, and traffic density with its collision risk [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]. Your job is to make the student find each of these in planning and decide what to do about it.

head: Hazard
How to manage it
rows: Class B floors and edges
Stay clear of the boundaries, especially where the floor is 3,000 feet AGL or less, and use the VFR Flyway Planning Chart [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-3]]
Flying under a Class C shelf
Expect aircraft without transponders or ADS-B below the 5 to 10 mile shelf [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]]
Radar service makes students passive
The pilot still owns the clearance and radio rules for B, C and D [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]], and ATC service does not relieve see and avoid, terrain clearance or VFR minimums [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]]
MOAs and MTRs
Fast, maneuvering military traffic; get status and advisories, or route around [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]] [[33:195|AIM 3-5-2]]
TFRs that appear on short notice
Check NOTAMs at every planning session; most TFRs are not on the chart [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]]
Busy training areas in haze
Crowded practice airspace and restricted visibility raise the collision hazard [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
Pressure to cut through
The wish to get somewhere on time can make a pilot ignore other hazards [[30:26|RMH 3-8]]

body.p: Your own risk is different: the student will meet this airspace alone. Build risk management in blocks [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]. In the cross-country phase, a private pilot's training can include flights in complex airspace, and the instructor should review and approve the learner's risk analysis for every dual and solo cross-country [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

callout.text: Your signature carries the risk. Class B solo needs training in that specific area and a 90-day endorsement [[60:287|14 CFR 61.95(a)]]. The pre-solo knowledge test must include the airspace rules for the solo airport, and you must review every wrong answer before the solo [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(b)]]. Write limits into the endorsement when needed; the student may not fly contrary to them [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(8)]].

check.q: Your student is getting flight following from a busy approach controller, with a Class D ahead. The student says 'approach will take care of the tower for me.' What do you teach?
check.a: The pilot is responsible for meeting the radio requirement before entering Class B, C or D, and keeps that responsibility while receiving radar advisories [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]]. Plan the tower call and ask approach for a frequency change in time.

body.p: Treat airspace as ground knowledge that pays off in flight. The AIH says ground objectives should be tied to flight objectives, and the instructor should point out the link between theory and practice [[25:172|AIH 9-2]].

bullets: Block 1, ground, home airspace only: the home airport's class, its tower hours, the vignette overhead, the practice area and the student limits of 61.89. Simple to complex: D, E and G first [[25:113|AIH 5-10]].
Block 2, ground, the chart: symbols practiced by themselves at the table before the student needs them in flight [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Use a current sectional and its legend.
Block 3, flight: demonstration-performance. Explain on the ground, demonstrate in the air while describing, supervise the student's performance, then evaluate [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
Radio entry into Class C or D with telling-and-doing: instructor tells and does the call, then learner tells while instructor does, then learner tells and does [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Block 4, scenario: give a cross-country with a Class B shelf, a MOA and a TFR. The student plans and decides; you act as mentor [[25:155|AIH 7-11]].
Reinforce: take learners to an ATC facility so they see the National Airspace System from the other side [[25:172|AIH 9-2]].
Review in short, regularly spaced sessions; they beat cramming [[25:92|AIH 3-41]].

callout.text: What to say before, during and after. Before: the objective ('today you will enter the Class C on your own call') and the standard. During: as few words as possible; let the student make the call and fly. After: the student assesses the flight first, then you compare it with your own assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]].

Teaching risk: heads-down chart reading and fumbled radio calls in busy airspace. Brief who is flying while the student reads the chart, and use the positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Have frequencies set and the chart reviewed before entering a high-density area such as Class B [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

check.q: Where on the sectional does the student find the frequency to call before entering a Class C, and about how far out?
check.a: In the magenta box notes giving the approach control frequency for arriving VFR aircraft, generally used within 20 NM [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Enters Class C or D without contact
Keeps going after 'Aircraft calling, standby'
No call sign in the reply means no contact; hold outside and call again [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]]
Treats 'radar contact' as a Class B clearance
Crosses the solid blue line on flight following
Only an ATC clearance opens Class B [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]] [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]]
Misreads floors and ceilings
Plans an altitude inside a shelf or above a Class D box value
Re-teach the '+', minus and 'T' symbols at the table [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]] [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Takes 'no NOTAM' to mean SUA is cold
Routes through a restricted area during its listed times
Read the chart tabulation; permanent times get no NOTAM [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]]
Forgets equipment rules not on the chart
No plan for the rules above Class C or at 10,000 MSL
Have the student list them in every plan [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]]
Uses the 1 SM Class G minimum for a solo
Solo plan accepts 2 SM
Applies Class E minimums at the Class E base
Cruises exactly at the floor and uses the higher class's rules
At the base you are in the airspace below [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]]
Uses an old chart or database
Expired tablet data or an old paper chart in the bag
Check edition dates at every preflight [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]] [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]]
Skips the TFR check
No NOTAM review in the briefing
TFR check on every flight [[33:195|AIM 3-5-3]] [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]]

check.q: A Class B sector is labeled 70 over +29. Is your student at 2,900 feet MSL inside Class B?
check.a: No. A '+' before the floor means the floor is above that value, and operations at and below it are outside Class B [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]]. Remind the student to keep a margin anyway [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: Class C, D and E on the legend

body.p: Teach the student to read each airspace symbol as a full sentence. A magenta 48 over 30 is a Class C that runs from 3,000 up to 4,800 feet MSL: the figures are in hundreds of feet MSL, with the last two zeros dropped [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]]. The most common misread is to say 'forty-eight feet' or to treat the numbers as feet above the ground.

A blue dashed Class D has its ceiling in a box. A minus sign in front, as in -27, means from the surface up to but not including 2,700 feet MSL [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]]. Students often skip the minus and think the box is a floor. A small inner box that says 'Class D excluded below 1500' MSL' means that small area is not Class D under that altitude; do not let the student treat the whole dashed outline as Class D to the surface [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

For Class E, teach the color of the vignette. A narrow magenta vignette is a 700-foot AGL floor; a blue vignette is a 1,200-foot AGL floor that abuts Class G [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]]. A 'CEILING' note appears along a limit only when the ceiling is below 18,000 feet MSL [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]]. Do not let the student read these as altitudes MSL; the vignette floors are above the ground.

The magenta box in the Class C example gives the approach frequency to call, generally within 20 NM, before entering [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]]. Have your student call it out: 'Contact Burbank Approach on 124.6.' Then ask what the regulation requires before entry: two-way radio communications, not a clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)]].

callout.text: Ask the student to point to a number on the chart and say the unit out loud: 'hundreds of feet MSL' or 'feet AGL'. A wrong unit is the error that follows a student into the cockpit.

scenario.title: Planning Maya's long solo cross-country
scenario.setup: You instruct at a towered (Class D) airport 22 NM from a Class B primary airport, inside its 30 NM veil. Your student Maya has 41 hours, a current solo endorsement and her solo cross-country training. Tomorrow she plans a solo cross-country to a nontowered airport 60 NM away. The direct line passes under a Class B shelf with a 4,000-foot MSL floor, clips the corner of a MOA listed on the chart as active 0800 to 1700 weekdays, and passes 6 NM from a city where a NOTAM shows a 91.141 VIP TFR from 1300 to 1600. The terrain is near 500 feet MSL. Forecast: 6 SM in the morning, 4 SM in haze by afternoon, scattered clouds at 3,500 feet AGL. The trainer has a Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out.

questions.q: Maya asks to fly straight through the Class B to save time. What would that take?
questions.a: A student needs ground and flight training in that specific Class B area and your endorsement dated within the 90 days before the flight [[60:287|14 CFR 61.95(a)]], plus an ATC clearance before entering [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]]. Without that training the answer is no; plan the route under or around it, with a margin from the floor [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-3]].

questions.q: She plans 3,500 feet MSL under the 4,000-foot shelf. With cloud bases at 3,500 feet AGL over terrain near 500 feet MSL, what do you point out?
questions.a: The cloud bases are near 4,000 feet MSL (500 + 3,500), so at 3,500 MSL she is exactly at the 500-foot below-cloud minimum for Class E below 10,000 MSL, with no margin [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]], and 500 feet under the Class B floor, where the AIM warns against flying too close [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-3]]. Look for a different route or plan.

questions.q: Afternoon haze is forecast at 4 SM. Is that legal for her, and what would change at night?
questions.a: 4 SM meets the Class E and G day minimums [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]] and the student limit of 3 SM by day; at night a student needs 5 SM [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(6)]]. Landing back in the Class D surface area also needs 3 SM ground visibility [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]].

questions.q: The MOA corner will be active during her flight. What do you teach and decide?
questions.a: VFR flight through an active MOA is allowed with extreme caution after getting status from an FSS within 100 miles and advisories from the controlling agency [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]]. For a solo student, a route around it is the simpler mitigation, and you may write that limit into her endorsement [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(8)]].

questions.q: How does she find the VIP TFR, and what is the rule?
questions.a: From the NOTAMs or the FAA TFR website during planning [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]] [[33:195|AIM 3-5-3]]; it will not be on her chart [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]]. No one may fly in the area contrary to the restrictions in the NOTAM [[60:459|14 CFR 91.141]].

questions.q: After the flight, how do you debrief the airspace decisions?
questions.a: Use collaborative assessment: Maya assesses herself first, then you compare it with your assessment [[25:176|AIH 9-6]]. After solo flights the learner should debrief the instructor on the risk management of the flight [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

skills.do: The examiner will have you "Identify and comply with the requirements for basic VFR weather minimums and flying in particular classes of airspace" (ACS AI.II.G.S1), and you demonstrate and explain at the same time. Expect to state the 91.155 minimums for any class, altitude and time of day the examiner names, the surface area ceiling and visibility rules and the student pilot limits, and to show how you teach a student to pick the right row from a METAR. This Task has no numeric tolerance; the standard is correct, complete and well taught.
skills.practice: Draw the 91.155 table from memory and add the 61.89 student limits beside it [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]] [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(6)]]. Have another applicant give you random positions, altitudes and METARs, and teach the decision out loud.

skills.do: The examiner will have you "Correctly identify airspace and operate in accordance with associated communication and equipment requirements" (ACS AI.II.G.S2). Expect a sectional: name each airspace on a route with its floor and ceiling, state the clearance or radio contact and the transponder and ADS-B Out needed, including the rules not drawn on the chart, and show how you teach a student the entry call.
skills.practice: Pick a route near a Class B on a current sectional and TAC and brief it as a lesson: symbols [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]], equipment [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]] and radio rules [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]]. Role-play the Class C call using telling-and-doing [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

skills.do: The examiner will have you "Identify the requirements for operating in SUA or within a TFR. Identify and comply with special air traffic rules (SATR) and SFRA operations, if applicable" (ACS AI.II.G.S3). Expect to read the chart's SUA tabulation, say which areas a VFR pilot may enter and how to get status, decode a TFR NOTAM, and explain the DC SFRA requirements and Special Awareness Training.
skills.practice: Pull current NOTAMs for your area, find a TFR, and brief who may enter under its 14 CFR section [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137]]. Read the SUA table on your sectional [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]] and walk another applicant through 93.339 [[60:705|14 CFR 93.339(a)]].

quiz.q: With no tower, what must an airport have before its surface area can be Class E?
options: Weather reporting and radio coverage down to the runway
An instrument approach with a published missed approach
A part-time tower that opens at least once a day
A UNICOM operator on duty during daylight hours
quiz.why: To qualify for a Class E surface area, the airport must have weather observation and reporting capability, and communications capability must exist with aircraft down to the runway surface [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].

quiz.q: The tower at your field closes at 2100. What happens to the 700-foot Class E transition area around it?
options: It closes with the tower and becomes Class G
It stays in effect, whatever the airport hours
It drops to the surface until the tower reopens
It rises to 1,200 feet AGL overnight
quiz.why: Class E transition areas beginning at 700 or 1,200 feet AGL are in effect regardless of airport operating hours or surface area status [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].

quiz.q: Over high terrain where no lower Class E base is charted, which airspace does the AIM leave out of the Class E that starts at 14,500 feet MSL?
options: Anything within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport
Anything over terrain that rises higher than 10,000 feet MSL
Below 1,500 feet above the surface, unless designated lower
Anything below 1,200 feet AGL along federal airways
quiz.why: Where nothing lower is designated, Class E starts at 14,500 feet MSL but does not include the airspace below 1,500 feet above the surface unless specifically designated lower, for example in mountainous terrain higher than 13,000 feet MSL [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].

quiz.q: How often are sectional charts updated in the conterminous U.S.?
options: Every 28 days
Once a year
Every 56 days
Every six months
quiz.why: The AIM and the Chart Users' Guide both say every 56 days [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]] [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]]. The PHAK's 'semiannually' is outdated [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]].

quiz.q: At what time do new charts and aeronautical information take effect in the U.S.?
options: Local midnight
quiz.why: 0901Z is the changeover time, chosen for its historically lower traffic [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]].

quiz.q: On a sectional, an airport symbol printed in blue means the airport:
options: Is inside Class B airspace
Is a private-use airport
Has fuel available
Has a control tower
quiz.why: Airports with control towers are shown in blue, all others in magenta [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]].

quiz.q: A restricted area extends from the surface to FL 300. What part of it does the VFR sectional show?
options: Only the part below 18,000 feet MSL
The full height to FL 300, with the top labeled
None of it, since it reaches into Class A
Only the part below 10,000 feet MSL
quiz.why: For special use airspace, VFR charts show only the airspace effective below 18,000 feet MSL [[2:45|Chart Users' Guide p.45]]. The chart's SUA tabulation gives the altitudes, times of use and controlling agency [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]].

quiz.q: Your student wants special VFR out of a Class E surface area at an airport with no tower. Who issues the clearance?
options: Only the nearest tower
UNICOM
The nearest tower, FSS or center
No clearance is needed in Class E
quiz.why: In a Class E surface area, a clearance may come from the nearest tower, FSS or center [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

quiz.q: A TRSA is best described as:
options: Non-part 71 airspace where VFR radar service is voluntary
A kind of Class C airspace with a smaller core
A restricted area set aside for radar testing
A type of SFRA with its own transponder code
quiz.why: TRSAs are not in part 71 or part 91 and do not fit any class; VFR participation is voluntary [[33:201|AIM 3-5-6]].

quiz.q: In Class D, what separation does ATC give between VFR aircraft?
options: None; no separation services are provided to VFR aircraft
500 feet of vertical separation from every other VFR aircraft
Standard radar separation, once radar contact is made
Separation only for student pilots who request it
quiz.why: In Class D, no separation services are provided to VFR aircraft [[33:187|AIM 3-2-5]]. Seeing and avoiding stays with the pilot.

quiz.q: The legend shows a magenta Class C ceiling of 48 over a floor of 30. What does your student write on the plan?
options: Floor 300 feet and ceiling 480 feet AGL
Floor 3,000 feet and ceiling 4,800 feet AGL
Floor 30 feet, ceiling 48 feet MSL
Floor 3,000 feet and ceiling 4,800 feet MSL
quiz.why: Class C altitudes are in hundreds of feet MSL: 48 is 4,800 and 30 is 3,000 [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

quiz.q: A blue dashed Class D shows a boxed ceiling of -27. What does the minus sign tell the student?
options: From 2,700 feet MSL up to the base of Class A airspace
The ceiling is 27 feet above the ground at the airport
The ceiling is 2,700 feet below the surface elevation
From the surface up to but not including 2,700 feet MSL
quiz.why: A minus in front of the figure means from the surface to, but not including, that value, in hundreds of feet MSL [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

quiz.q: On the legend, a small box inside a Class D outline is labelled 'Class D excluded below 1500' MSL'. What is the correct reading?
options: Class D extends up to 1,500 feet MSL only in that box
Class D does not apply below 1,500 feet MSL in that box
The entire Class D area ends at 1,500 feet MSL overall
The small box is a restricted area up to 1,500 feet MSL
quiz.why: The legend shows the excluded area as a small box with the note that Class D is excluded below 1,500 feet MSL [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

quiz.q: A student finds a blue-shaded vignette bar along a boundary, like the third bar in the Class E legend. What does it mark?
options: Class E from the surface for an airport
The edge of a Class D surface area
A 700-foot AGL Class E floor next to a 1,200-foot area
A Class E floor of 1,200 feet AGL next to Class G
quiz.why: The legend ties the blue vignette to airspace beginning at 1,200 feet AGL that abuts Class G; the magenta vignettes are the 700-foot AGL floors [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

quiz.q: Your student is about to enter a charted Class C shelf with the radios set up and tuned. Which must happen before she enters?
options: She must squawk 7600 for the whole time in the shelf
She must establish two-way radio communications with ATC
She must file a VFR flight plan with flight service
She must receive a specific ATC clearance before entering
quiz.why: For arrival or through flight in Class C, the pilot must establish two-way radio communications before entering and maintain them. Class B is the one that needs a clearance [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)]].

final_quiz.q: At night, in Class G below 1,200 feet AGL, in the traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway, flight visibility is 2 SM. A private pilot and your solo student are each flying there. What is true?
options: Both are legal under the night pattern exception in 91.155(b)(2)
Neither is legal, since night Class G needs 3 SM everywhere
The private pilot is legal; the student is not, needing 5 SM at night
The student is legal because the pattern exception overrides 61.89
final_quiz.why: The 91.155(b)(2) exception allows clear of clouds with 1 to 3 SM in the pattern [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]], but a student pilot may not act as PIC with less than 5 SM at night [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(6)]].

final_quiz.q: You endorsed a student 75 days ago for solo flight at a specific airport inside Class B. She wants to go today, and again in three weeks. What is true?
options: Valid today; in three weeks it is over 90 days old, so she needs a new one
Valid both times, for 12 calendar months from the endorsement date
Invalid today, since a Class B airport endorsement lasts only 60 days
Valid both times, since solo endorsements last as long as the student certificate
final_quiz.why: The endorsement must be dated within the 90 days before the flight: 75 days today, 96 days in three weeks [[60:287|14 CFR 61.95(b)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: A student's tablet database expired last week and cannot be updated before the flight. What does the PHAK say to do?
options: Use it as is, since airspace rarely changes within a few weeks
Disregard its moving-map airspace for critical decisions; verify with current sources
Use it, but stay below 3,000 feet AGL until the update is done
Use it as long as ADS-B In weather and traffic are working
final_quiz.why: With an expired database, disregard moving-map airspace for critical navigation decisions and verify waypoints against a current sectional or Chart Supplement [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's solo route passes through an alert area. What applies?
options: Permission from the controlling agency before entering the area
An ATC clearance, as for a restricted area
Entry is prohibited while the area is active
Extra vigilance; all pilots there share collision avoidance
final_quiz.why: Alert areas warn of high-volume training or unusual activity; activity follows the CFRs without waiver, and everyone shares collision avoidance [[33:191|AIM 3-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: Between chart editions, how does the FAA tell users about an error found in a published chart?
options: It waits for the next 56-day edition and corrects it then
Only by NOTAM, since chart errors are never announced otherwise
A Safety Alert; planned changes come as Charting Notices
A Data Product Notice, which covers all chart errors
final_quiz.why: Safety Alerts notify users of an error reported or discovered in a product; Charting Notices announce a planned chart enhancement; Data Product Notices cover system outages [[34:190|AIM 9-1-3]].

final_quiz.q: You will do pattern work at a towered airport inside the DC SFRA but outside the FRZ. Unless ATC assigns another, which transponder code do you use?
final_quiz.why: In the VFR pattern at a towered airport in the SFRA, operate on code 1234 unless ATC assigns a different code [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(d)(3)]]. Code 1200 is never used in the SFRA [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].

final_quiz.q: Your private pilot client gets special VFR out of a Class D surface area and then leaves it. What separation does ATC give after that?
options: Separation from all VFR traffic within 20 NM
Full SVFR separation from all traffic until she climbs above 10,000 feet MSL
Separation from IFR traffic only, until she lands
None: SVFR separation is given only inside the surface area
final_quiz.why: ATC separates special VFR flights from each other and from IFR flights, but does not provide separation after an aircraft leaves the surface area on a special VFR clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: How does a sectional show an airport where fixed-wing special VFR is not allowed?
options: A red X through the airport symbol
'NO SVFR' printed above the airport name
A magenta box with the word SPECIAL
A dashed blue ring drawn around the airport symbol
final_quiz.why: Part 91 airports where fixed-wing special VFR operations are prohibited are shown with the type 'NO SVFR' above the airport name [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].

final_quiz.q: Your student finds an altitude reservation (ALTRV) NOTAM on the route. What does the AIM say about VFR flight through it?
options: Prohibited for all aircraft while the NOTAM is in effect
Permitted for nonparticipating VFR aircraft, with vigilance
Allowed only with a clearance from the CARF or the ARTCC that issued it
Allowed only above 10,000 feet MSL with a transponder
final_quiz.why: An ALTRV is announced by airspace NOTAM and keeps nonparticipating IFR aircraft separated from the activity; nonparticipating VFR aircraft may fly through the area but should exercise vigilance [[33:203|AIM 3-5-10]].

final_quiz.q: A student says: 'A VFR transition route is just like a flyway; no clearance needed.' What do you teach?
options: Correct: like a flyway, a transition route needs no clearance and no radio call at all
They need an SFRA flight plan filed before the flight
Transition routes are for IFR traffic only, so VFR may not use them
It needs ATC communication where it crosses B, C or D, and a clearance in Class B
final_quiz.why: Flyways need no clearance [[33:198|AIM 3-5-5]]; transition routes need ATC communication and, in Class B, a clearance [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your home airport has a part-time Class D that changes to Class G when the tower closes. Its arrival extensions are part of the surface area. After the tower closes, the extensions are:
options: Still Class E
Class G
Class D
Class E, but only below 700 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: For part-time Class D surface areas that change to Class G, the arrival extensions become Class G at the same time [[33:187|AIM 3-2-5]].

final_quiz.q: A student plans 9,500 feet MSL on a magnetic course of 270, about 4,000 feet above the ground. What is wrong?
options: Westbound above 3,000 feet AGL is even thousands plus 500, such as 8,500 or 10,500
Nothing: 9,500 feet is correct for any course above 3,000 feet AGL
No cruising altitude rule applies more than 3,000 feet above the ground
Westbound uses odd thousands plus 500, so 9,500 is fine
final_quiz.why: On magnetic courses 180 through 359, VFR cruise above 3,000 feet AGL is even thousands plus 500 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]]; 9,500 is an eastbound altitude [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: Your student's route passes close to a Class B. Which chart should she use near it, and why?
options: The IFR low altitude chart, since Class B is for IFR traffic
The Terminal Area Chart, which gives greater detail there
The sectional only, since the TAC leaves out the Class B layers
The Chart Supplement, which replaces charts near Class B
final_quiz.why: Sectionals mark TAC coverage with a masked line; within that area pilots should use TACs, which provide greater detail [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]] [[34:191|AIM 9-1-5]].

final_quiz.q: The legend shows a line with 'CEILING 14,000 MSL' above it and '8000 AGL' below it. Why is the 'CEILING' note printed?
options: It shows a minimum safe altitude over terrain and obstacles
It is printed because the ceiling is below 18,000 feet MSL
It marks the ceiling of Class G airspace beneath the line
It marks the top of Class A airspace at 14,000 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: The legend says the symbol differentiates floors above 700 feet AGL, and the word CEILING is shown when the ceiling is below 18,000 feet MSL [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

final_quiz.q: The magenta box on the legend reads 'CTC BURBANK APP WITHIN 20 NM ON 124.6 395.9'. Your student has a standard civil VHF radio. What do you teach her to do?
options: Call Burbank Approach on 124.6 before entering
Call on 395.9 because it is the clearer frequency
Call the tower on 124.6 only after landing
Wait for ATC to call her first inside the Class C
final_quiz.why: The box gives the approach control frequencies for arriving VFR aircraft to call before entering Class C, generally within 20 NM [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]]. The second number, 395.9, is a UHF frequency, not tunable on a civil VHF radio [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

final_quiz.q: You are flying VFR in a Class D area at a towered airport and the radio fails. Which set of conditions must you meet to land?
options: Basic VFR minimums, visual contact with the tower, and a landing clearance
Any weather minimums, as long as the transponder is squawking 7600
Basic VFR minimums, a call to the tower on the phone, and a landing light
Special VFR weather minimums, an ADS-B alert, and a clearance to land
final_quiz.why: With a VFR radio failure in Class D, the pilot may land only if weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, visual contact with the tower is kept, and a clearance to land is received [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)]].

takeaways: Frame first: categories, types and classes; where they overlap, the more restrictive rules win.
Class B needs a clearance; C and D need two-way contact, and your call sign in the reply is the key.
Student pilots: 3 SM by day and 5 SM at night, Class B solo only with area training and a 90-day endorsement, and some airports never.
Some equipment rules are not on the chart: above Class C and at or above 10,000 MSL.
No NOTAM does not mean SUA is cold, and most TFRs are not charted.
Charts change every 56 days at 0901Z; check the cover date and the database.
Teach simple to complex, symbols on the ground, and radio calls with telling-and-doing.
cfi_notes: The PHAK says sectionals and TACs are revised semiannually [[1:389|PHAK 16-2]]; the AIM and the Chart Users' Guide say every 56 days [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]] [[2:23|Chart Users' Guide p.23]]. Teach 56 days.

PHAK 15-3 says Class E begins at 14,500 feet MSL where no base is charted [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]], but leaves out the exclusion of airspace within 1,500 feet of the surface that the AIM and the Chart Users' Guide give [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]] [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]]. Over high terrain, Class G goes above 14,500 MSL.

AIM 4-4-6g says night fixed-wing SVFR needs an instrument-rated pilot [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]; the rule says the pilot must meet the applicable Part 61 requirements for instrument flight [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]]. Teach the CFR wording.

AIM 3-2-3 lists the primary airports where the PIC needs at least a private certificate to take off or land [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]]. The governing list is Part 91 Appendix D, section 4 [[60:650|14 CFR Part 91 App. D]]; check the CFR if the lists ever differ.
The CFR still calls it the Gulf of Mexico in 91.225(d)(5) [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(5)]], while the AIM says Gulf of America [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]]. Same airspace; expect students to ask.

Application: the AIH's advice to save Class A, B and C for later [[25:113|AIH 5-10]] has a limit. If the home airport sits under a Class B shelf or inside the veil, those rules belong in the pre-solo test, which must cover the airspace rules for the solo airport [[60:271|14 CFR 61.87(b)]].
Have students write their own study questions about the local airspace; the AIH reports better recall even when the questions are thrown away unanswered [[25:92|AIH 3-41]].

AC 61-65K's Class B endorsements end with '[List any applicable conditions or limitations]' [[12:42|AC 61-65K A-9]]. The sources do not say what limits to write; use them for things like weather, times or routes you trained.
Students quote PHAK Figure 15-9 as the whole rule [[1:384|PHAK 15-9]]. It is a summary; teach from 91.131, 91.215 and 91.225.
gaps: Local ATC procedures for pilot training at airports in Class B and local letters of agreement are not in these sources; 91.131 only says to comply with them [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(3)]].
Current NOTAMs, TFRs and the sectional for your own area are not in the sources; pull them live for every lesson.
Part 93 areas other than the DC SFRA are not taught here; read the part 93 subpart for any area you fly near.

An ADIZ is an area where the ready identification, location and control of all aircraft is required for national security [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]]; the part 99 ADIZ and DVFR rules themselves are not in these sources.
The sources give no standard way to grade a student's airspace knowledge; use your syllabus and the ACS for the certificate sought.

activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A Class D primary airport sits at 1,180 feet MSL. Its Class D has the general height of 2,500 feet above the airport. What is the top, in feet MSL?
items.why: 1,180 + 2,500 = 3,680 feet MSL. Class D generally goes from the surface to 2,500 feet above airport elevation, charted in MSL [[33:185|AIM 3-2-5]]. The chart's box gives the real value.

items.q: A nontowered airport at 850 feet MSL lies inside a magenta vignette. At what altitude, in feet MSL, does Class E begin overhead?
items.why: A magenta vignette means a 700-foot AGL floor [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]]: 850 + 700 = 1,550 feet MSL.

items.q: Terrain under your route is 8,200 feet MSL. Up to what MSL altitude does the 'at and below 2,500 feet AGL' exclusion from the en route transponder and ADS-B Out rules still apply?
items.why: 8,200 + 2,500 = 10,700 feet MSL. Above that, at and above 10,000 MSL, both are required [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]].

items.q: A sectional edition took effect on September 4. Sectionals are updated every 56 days. On what day of October does the next edition take effect?
items.why: September has 30 days, so September 4 + 26 days = September 30, and 30 more days = October 30 (26 + 30 = 56) [[34:190|AIM 9-1-5]].

items.q: In a Class D surface area you fly the pattern at 1,000 feet AGL. What is the lowest cloud base, in feet AGL, that keeps the required distance below clouds?
items.why: Class D needs 500 feet below clouds: 1,000 + 500 = 1,500 feet AGL [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. A ceiling also must be at least 1,000 feet to fly VFR beneath it in a surface area [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]].

activities.title: True or false: charts and their currency
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: An obsolete sectional is fine for VFR as long as you also check NOTAMs.
cards.why: False. Use current editions and discard obsolete charts and publications [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]].

cards.s: The next scheduled edition date is printed on the chart cover.
cards.why: True. That is how to confirm a chart is current [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]].

cards.s: SUA active at its permanently listed times gets a NOTAM each day.
cards.why: False. No NOTAM is issued to announce permanently listed times of use [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]].

cards.s: Alert areas do not extend into Class A, B, C or D airspace or Class E surface areas.
cards.why: True, as the chart guide notes [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].

cards.s: The Chart Supplement is issued every 56 days.
On the sectional, the names of Part 93 airports are boxed.
cards.why: True. Airports and heliports under Part 93 special air traffic rules are shown by boxing the airport name [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].

cards.s: Temporary restricted areas are drawn on the sectional.
cards.why: False. Temporary restricted areas are not charted [[33:191|AIM 3-4-3]].

activities.title: Dual cross-country into Class C
activities.intro: You are flying dual with a 30-hour student from a nontowered field to a Class C airport 40 NM away. A Class B shelf lies off to the east.

steps.s: Preflight. The student says the sectional is current because it 'looks new.' What do you have the student do?
options: Accept it as current, since a clean cover and crisp folds show it is the newest edition
Ask the tower on the radio whether the chart edition is still current before engine start
Read the next edition date on the cover and pull NOTAMs
Check only the GPS database date and treat the paper chart as a backup reference
steps.why: Confirm currency from the next scheduled edition date on the cover, and check NOTAMs for changes between editions [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p.6]].

steps.s: Twenty-five NM out, the student asks when to call approach.
options: At the Class C boundary, then wait for the controller to call you before going further
Not until the tower calls you, since approach only talks to aircraft it already has on radar
Only after hearing the ATIS twice and writing down the altimeter setting and runway in use
Far enough out that two-way radio is established before entering
steps.why: Call far enough from the boundary to avoid entering before two-way radio communication is established [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].

steps.s: The controller answers with your call sign and 'standby.' The student starts a turn away from the Class C.
options: Good call; standby means stay out
Contact is made; you may enter the Class C
You still need a clearance to enter
Squawk 1200 and leave the frequency
steps.why: If the controller responds with your call sign and 'standby,' radio communication is established and you may enter Class C [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].

steps.s: Approach sets you up for a visual approach below the Class C shelf. What should the student expect down there?
options: Non-transponder, non-ADS-B VFR aircraft, so keep scanning
Only aircraft talking to approach, since everyone below the shelf must call
No other traffic, since the shelf area is closed to VFR
Only IFR traffic flying the instrument approach
steps.why: Aircraft below the 5 to 10 mile shelf during an instrument or visual approach may encounter non-transponder and non-ADS-B VFR aircraft [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].

steps.s: For the trip home, the student plans to cruise just under the Class B shelf, whose floor is 2,500 feet AGL, to save time. What do you say?
options: Fine; just under the floor is outside Class B, so there is no concern as long as you stay below 2,500 feet AGL and keep clear of clouds
Climb into the Class B without a clearance, since you are on flight following and the controller already has your route
Stay well clear of the boundary, especially where the floor is 3,000 feet or less; plan with the VFR Flyway Planning Chart
Descend to 500 feet AGL under the shelf so you are far below the floor and out of every controller's way
steps.why: VFR aircraft near Class B are cautioned against operating too closely to its boundaries, especially where the floor is 3,000 feet or less [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]]; VFR Flyway Planning Charts are on the back of the TACs [[33:182|AIM 3-2-3]].

activities.why: Where designations overlap, the more restrictive rules apply; 71.9 ranks Class A first, then B, C, D and E, with Class G least restrictive [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]].
